parsed_answer.content: In high-concurrency distributed systems, Cache Breakdown and Cache Avalanche are critical failure modes that occur when the caching layer fails to shield the underlying database from a surge in traffic. Cache Breakdown (often called 'hotspot invalidation') happens when a specific, highly popular key expires, causing a massive influx of concurrent requests to hit the database simultaneously to recompute the value. Cache Avalanche is a more systemic failure where a large cluster of cache keys expires at the same time, or the entire cache node goes offline, leading to a catastrophic 'thundering herd' effect that can crash the database due to connection pool exhaustion and CPU saturation.

items: To mitigate Cache Breakdown, implement 'Mutex Locking' (or distributed locks via Redis SETNX) to ensure only one thread recomputes the value while others wait or return a stale value.
To prevent Cache Avalanche, apply 'Jitter' or 'Randomized Expiration' to your TTLs, ensuring that keys do not expire at the exact same timestamp.
Utilize 'Logical Expiration' where the cache entry contains an explicit timestamp, allowing the application to serve stale data while an asynchronous thread refreshes the cache.
Implement circuit breakers (e.g., Resilience4j) to fail fast when the database latency exceeds a threshold, preventing the application from hanging on blocked I/O threads.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap is setting a fixed TTL for all keys in a cache. If you load 10,000 keys at startup, they will all expire simultaneously 60 minutes later. Always add a random jitter (e.g., +/- 10%) to your TTLs to spread the load across the timeline.
